clue.text: Coherent American serving in pub

indicators.note: someone serving in a place is stationed inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: your local is your nearest pub
a GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A sensible American is working behind the bar of a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Serving looks like pulling pints, but it is soldiering. A local is the British term for one's regular neighbourhood pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A coherent argument is a reasoned one that hangs together, which is what logical describes.

clue.text: Dropping ecstasy, US singer looked angry

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, so that letter is taken out of the name

blocks.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
Lou Reed, the American singer of the Velvet Underground

explanation.surface: An American rock star gives up drugs and scowls.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the E from LOU REED leaves LOURED.
explanation.definitionFit: To lour (or lower) is to frown or scowl, so loured is a past-tense verb meaning glowered.

clue.text: Contagious virus – complaint with extra power

indicators.note: something extra is added into the word, here slotted in among its letters

blocks.note: a gripe is a grumble
P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: Catching an infectious bug is a complaint with real force.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads complaint as an illness; it is a grumble, with the extra P placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Grippe is an old name, borrowed from French, for influenza, an infectious viral illness.

clue.text: Unfairly select pop diva track still on the radio

indicators.note: what is on the radio is heard rather than seen, so the spelling follows the sound

blocks.note: Cher, the singer
RY is short for railway
a still is a photograph, a pic

explanation.surface: A DJ unfairly favours a particular diva's song, still being played on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Track looks like a song and still like 'even now'; they are the railway and a photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: To cherry-pick is to choose only the most favourable items, a biased kind of selection.

clue.text: Lizzie's jacket fitting Rose remarkably

indicators.note: a jacket is the outer layer, so only the outside letters of the name are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of Lizzie
fitting means suitable, apt

explanation.surface: Elizabeth's coat suits a woman called Rose remarkably well.
explanation.walkthrough: Rose looks like a woman's name, but it is the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: Leapt is a past-tense verb for jumping up, a sudden and striking way of rising.

clue.text: Work repeatedly to save part of hospital with no roof

indicators.note: to save something is to hold onto it, so the pieces wrap around another

blocks.note: OP is short for opus, a work
the ear, nose and throat department
the work is given a second time

explanation.surface: Hospital staff keep working on a ward whose roof has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Repeatedly asks for OP twice, and the pair holds ENT: OP-ENT-OP.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-top vehicle, such as a sightseeing bus, has no roof over its passengers.

clue.text: Old fellows with lots of cash getting dumped

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
F for fellow, doubled for the plural
loaded means very rich

explanation.surface: Elderly wealthy men find themselves being dumped by their partners.
explanation.definitionFit: To offload is to get rid of something unwanted, so offloaded is a synonym for dumped.

clue.text: Old French bread and sauce American leaves out

definitions.note: bread is a mass noun here; the answer is plural coins

indicators.note: whatever leaves is no longer there, so that letter goes
out can mean wrong or disordered, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
A is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: An American skips the sauce and has plain French bread.
explanation.walkthrough: Bread looks like food, but it is slang for money: the écu was an old French coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecus were historical French coins, and bread is slang for money, so old French money fits.

clue.text: Pious hairstyles certainly embraced by many

indicators.note: what is embraced is held in someone's arms, so it sits inside the other word

blocks.note: tons means lots
sure as an emphatic yes

explanation.surface: Religious haircuts are, of course, popular with many people.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonsure is the shaved crown worn by monks, a haircut adopted for religious devotion.

clue.text: Sunak welcoming sale on modified foreign imports, say

indicators.note: something modified has been changed, so these letters are rearranged
to welcome someone is to take them in, so the outer piece goes around the rest

blocks.note: Rishi Sunak was Prime Minister
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister welcomes a discount on altered goods brought in from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an example: imports are foreign by nature, so the phrase says the same thing twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleonasm is a redundant use of words, as in calling imports foreign when that is already implied.

clue.text: Waste hour in Ealing? Not all of it

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, so the answer sits inside the run of letters

blocks.note: inside hoUR IN Ealing

explanation.surface: Wasting an hour in a London suburb, though not the whole of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Ealing is a district of west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Urine is the liquid waste the body passes, so waste works as a general term for it.

clue.text: Having cash to flash, a dodgy dealer catches 2

indicators.note: to catch something is to trap it, so the dealer surrounds the illness

blocks.note: taken as written
a fence deals in stolen goods
2 refers to the answer at 2 Down, a name for influenza

explanation.surface: A shady dealer with money to show off catches a nasty bug.
explanation.walkthrough: The bare number is a cross-reference: it stands for the answer at 2 Down, whose everyday name supplies the inner piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Affluence is wealth, the state of having plenty of money to spend and show off.

clue.text: Old detective, one entering shop for a wheeze, say

indicators.note: something entering goes inside, so the single letter is placed within the verb

blocks.note: ex means former
a private investigator
to shop someone is to rat on them
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A retired sleuth breaks into a shop as some clever scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: Shop is a verb, British slang for informing on someone; wheeze looks like a scheme but is a breath.
explanation.definitionFit: Expiration is breathing out, and a wheeze is one noisy example of an outgoing breath.

clue.text: Scottish writer cutting the BS and the pot

indicators.note: cutting things means removing them, here the named letters

blocks.note: Robert Burns, the Scottish poet
the letters B and S to be removed

explanation.surface: A Scottish author drops the nonsense and the drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: BS looks like slang for nonsense and pot like cannabis; one names two letters, the other a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: An urn is a large vase or pot, often for ashes or for serving tea.

clue.text: Sixty engineers stopping a source of excitement on match day

indicators.note: something stopping a hole plugs it, so it sits inside the phrase

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers

blocks.clueFragment: a source of excitement on match day
blocks.note: fans keep checking the current score

explanation.surface: Sixty engineers block a thrilling moment on the day of the game.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is twenty, so three of them make the archaic number sixty.

clue.text: Maybe Marge Simpson's opening these funny programs

indicators.note: an opening is the start, so only the first letter of the surname is used
funny means peculiar, so the letters are rearranged oddly

blocks.note: marge, short for margarine, is a spread
the first letter of Simpson
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Marge from The Simpsons launches some comic television shows.
explanation.walkthrough: Marge Simpson is the cartoon mother, but marge is British shorthand for margarine.
explanation.definitionFit: Spreadsheets are software applications, so programs (computer sense) covers them.

clue.text: English setter better without clothing decoration

indicators.note: a word stripped of clothing has lost its outer layer, so only its inside remains

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
Paul is a fellow Guardian crossword setter
the inside letters of better

explanation.surface: An English crossword setter, better off undressed, says something about ornament.
explanation.walkthrough: Setter looks like a dog, but it is a crossword compiler, here Paul from the same paper.
explanation.definitionFit: An epaulette is an ornamental shoulder piece on a uniform, a decoration worn on clothing.

clue.text: Speaks incoherently, even leaving S Club 7

indicators.note: what is leaving departs, so those letters are taken out of the number word

blocks.note: taken as written
a putter is a golf club
the letters to remove
the number written as a word

explanation.surface: Someone mumbles nonsense, even as they quit a pop group.
explanation.walkthrough: S Club 7 is a British pop group, but the name splits apart: even is an instruction acting on the number written out in words.
explanation.definitionFit: To sputter is to speak in hasty, spluttering bursts, which comes out incoherent.

clue.text: Performed start of play, Chekhov's first with a message

indicators.note: first means the opening letter only of the playwright's name is used

blocks.note: did as in carried out
a play begins with Act I
the first letter of Chekhov

explanation.surface: A theatre company performed the opening of a Chekhov play, which carried a moral.
explanation.walkthrough: Start of play looks like a letter-selection clue for P, but it is the opening act, Act I.
explanation.definitionFit: Didactic means intended to teach, so a didactic work carries a moral or instructive lesson.

clue.text: Nerd with new Capri pants, not a sweater?

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are a mess to be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A geek in fresh capri trousers asks whether he avoids wearing a jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants look like the trousers but are the signal; the royal claimed in a 2019 TV interview that he could not sweat.
explanation.definitionFit: The prince said a medical condition left him unable to perspire, so he is jokingly someone who does not sweat.

clue.text: It's heard in Kabul at posh parties

indicators.note: parties is read as a verb, splitting up and dividing, so the letters are broken and rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Talk overheard at smart gatherings in Afghanistan's capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Pashto is one of Afghanistan's official languages, spoken by many people in Kabul.

clue.text: Swiss banker, briefly working, gets indicator of time

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: Zurich bankers are nicknamed the gnomes of Zurich
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A Swiss banker, putting in short hours, acquires a timepiece.
explanation.definitionFit: A gnomon is the pin on a sundial whose shadow shows the hour.

clue.text: Only half of teachers as keen to get sweet food

indicators.note: only half of each word is kept, its front portion, and the rest discarded

blocks.note: the first four of its eight letters
the first of its two letters
the first two of its four letters

explanation.surface: Only half the teaching staff are eager for a sweet treat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests half of the teachers as people; it means the first half of each word that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacake is a sweet bun, often with dried fruit, served toasted and buttered.

clue.text: Drop of claret is too bland when drunk

indicators.note: drunk means intoxicated and unsteady, so the letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A wine critic finds a sip of Bordeaux lacking flavour once drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Claret looks like the wine, but it is old boxing slang for blood.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloodstain is the mark left by a drop of blood, and claret is slang for blood.

clue.text: Marx, after revolution, becoming media personality

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the name is read the other way

blocks.note: Harpo Marx, one of the Marx Brothers

explanation.surface: Following the revolution, Marx becomes a TV star.
explanation.walkthrough: Marx points to Karl and revolution, but it is Harpo of the comedy Marx Brothers.
explanation.definitionFit: Oprah Winfrey is a famous American talk-show host and television personality.

clue.text: See 21 Across
Spear carrier hasn't finished with e.g. Brad Pitt fan?

indicators.note: something not finished lacks its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a spear carrier is a non-speaking extra on stage
Brad Pitt is an example of a film actor

explanation.surface: A bit-part player who hasn't made it is an admirer of a Hollywood star.
explanation.walkthrough: Fan suggests an admirer of Brad Pitt; it is an electric fan that draws out air.
explanation.definitionFit: An extractor fan removes stale air or steam, so a fan can be an example of one.

clue.text: Ancient characters travel westwards with unsubtle performer

indicators.note: in an across answer westwards means right to left, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: to go is to travel
a ham is an over-the-top actor

explanation.surface: Elderly characters head west with a hammy actor.
explanation.walkthrough: Characters look like people in a story; they are letters of an old alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogham is an early Irish alphabet of strokes cut on stone, so its letters are ancient characters.

clue.text: Conceal what tourists may do in Greece, losing energy once

indicators.note: losing something means it is gone, so that letter is removed from the phrase
once limits the loss to a single occurrence, since the phrase holds the letter twice

blocks.clueFragment: what tourists may do in Greece
blocks.note: visitors might see Crete, a Greek island
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Hiding what holidaymakers get up to in Greece after their stamina has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: Crete is a Greek island; of the two E letters in the phrase, only one goes.
explanation.definitionFit: To secrete something is to hide it away, a less common sense than producing a fluid.

clue.text: Oddly, Hoover now wild about Democratic Party in US

indicators.note: oddly means taking the letters in odd-numbered positions only
wild means out of control, so the letters are rearranged
about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go round the abbreviation

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters
the letters to rearrange
D is the abbreviation for Democratic

explanation.surface: Strangely, a Hoover now goes crazy over the Democratic Party in America.
explanation.walkthrough: Hoover suggests the US president and Party the political party; it is a barn-dance party.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoedown is an American country dance or party with folk music and square dancing.
